e-3131.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
e-3131.problem: Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,\pi)$ given that $f(x,y) = (x - y)\cos y.$
e-3131.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the gradient at the specified point, we substitute $(x,y)= (1,\pi)$ into the above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(1,\pi ) & ={f}_{x}(1,\pi )\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(1,\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +(1-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3132.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
e-3132.problem: Evaluate $\nabla g(x,y,z)$   at $(2,-1,3)$ if $g(x,y,z) = x^2 + xyz.$
e-3132.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =2x+yz \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xz \\  & =xz \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xy \\  & =xy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+(xz)\text{ }j+(xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇g(2,-1,3) & =(2(2)+(-1)(3))\text{ }i+2(3)\text{ }j+2(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =1\text{ }i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3133.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
e-3133.problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y-4)\ln (x-2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
e-3133.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$

e-3150.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
e-3150.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
e-3150.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Evaluate ∇h(x,y) at (1,1) if h(x,y)=4xarctan⁡y.

a
 ⟨π,12⟩
b
 ⟨π,2⟩
c
 ⟨π4,12⟩
d
 ⟨2π,0⟩
e
 ⟨1,1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: The partial derivatives are h_x=4\arctan(y) and h_y=4x/(1+y^2). At (1,1), these equal π and 2, so ∇h(1,1)=⟨π,2⟩.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Evaluate ∇h(x,y) at (1,1) if h(x,y)=4xarctan⁡y.

a
 ⟨π,12⟩
b
 ⟨π,2⟩
c
 ⟨π4,12⟩
d
 ⟨2π,0⟩
e
 ⟨1,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives hx(x,y)=∂∂x(4xarctan⁡y)=4arctan⁡yhy(x,y)=∂∂y(4xarctan⁡y)=4xy2+1 Hence, the gradient is ∇h(x,y)=⟨hx(x,y),hy(x,y)⟩=⟨4arctan⁡y,4xy2+1⟩∇h(1,1)=⟨4arctan⁡1,4⋅112+1⟩=⟨4⋅π4,42⟩=⟨π,2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 16 i+12 j

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =8x-3y+0+0 \\  & =8x-3y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =0-3x+4y+1 \\  & =4y-3x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & ={h}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =(8x-3y)\text{ }i+(4y-3x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇h(2,3) & =(8\cdot 2-3\cdot 3)\text{ }i+(4\cdot 3-3\cdot 2+1)\text{ }j \\  & =7\text{ }i+7\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Evaluate ∇h(x,y) at (2,3) if h(x,y)=4x2−3xy+2y2+y.

a
 16 i+12 j
b
 9 i+12 j
c
 16 i+6 j
d
 9 i−6 j
e
 7 i+7 j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

hx(x,y)=∂∂x(4x2−3xy+2y2+y)=8x−3y+0+0=8x−3yhy(x,y)=∂∂y(4x2−3xy+2y2+y)=0−3x+4y+1=4y−3x+1

Hence, the gradient is:

∇h(x,y)=hx(x,y) i+hy(x,y) j=(8x−3y) i+(4y−3x+1) j∇h(2,3)=(8⋅2−3⋅3) i+(4⋅3−3⋅2+1) j=7 i+7 j

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares 7i+7j, matching option e. Independently, h_x(2,3)=16-9=7 and h_y(2,3)=12-6+1=7, confirming that result.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =8x-3y+0+0 \\  & =8x-3y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =0-3x+4y+1 \\  & =4y-3x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & ={h}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =(8x-3y)\text{ }i+(4y-3x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇h(2,3) & =(8\cdot 2-3\cdot 3)\text{ }i+(4\cdot 3-3\cdot 2+1)\text{ }j \\  & =7\text{ }i+7\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

If h(x,y)=arctan⁡(yx), find ∇h(x,y).

a
 xx2+y2i−yx2+y2j
b
 −xx2+y2i+yx2+y2j
c
 yx2+y2i−xx2+y2j
d
 −yx2+y2i+xx2+y2j
e
 −y2x2+y2i+x2x2+y2j
Submit

decision.explanation: By the chain rule, h_x=(-y/x²)/(1+(y/x)²)=-y/(x²+y²) and h_y=(1/x)/(1+(y/x)²)=x/(x²+y²), for x≠0. These are the components of the gradient, matching option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

If h(x,y)=arctan⁡(yx), find ∇h(x,y).

a
 xx2+y2i−yx2+y2j
b
 −xx2+y2i+yx2+y2j
c
 yx2+y2i−xx2+y2j
d
 −yx2+y2i+xx2+y2j
e
 −y2x2+y2i+x2x2+y2j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂x(arctan⁡(yx))=11+(yx)2⋅(−yx2)=x2x2+y2⋅(−yx2)=−yx2+y2fy(x,y)=∂∂y(arctan⁡(yx))=11+(yx)2⋅(1x)=x2x2+y2⋅1x=xx2+y2

Hence, the gradient is ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=−yx2+y2i+xx2+y2j.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Evaluate ∇f(x,y) at (2,1) if f(x,y)=x2y+3.

a
 ⟨1,8⟩
b
 ⟨8,1⟩
c
 ⟨16,1⟩
d
 ⟨4,12⟩
e
 ⟨2,0⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: f_x=2x√(y+3) and f_y=x²/(2√(y+3)). At (2,1), these equal 8 and 1, respectively, so ∇f(2,1)=⟨8,1⟩.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),\,{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\sqrt{y+3},\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}⟩ \\ ∇f(2,1) & =⟨2\cdot 2\sqrt{1+3},\,\frac{{2}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1+3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,1⟩\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

Evaluate ∇f(x,y) at (2,1) if f(x,y)=x2y+3.

a
 ⟨1,8⟩
b
 ⟨8,1⟩
c
 ⟨16,1⟩
d
 ⟨4,12⟩
e
 ⟨2,0⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

fx(x,y)=∂∂x(x2y+3)=2xy+3fy(x,y)=∂∂y(x2y+3)=x22y+3. Hence, the gradient is:

∇f(x,y)=⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨2xy+3,x22y+3⟩∇f(2,1)=⟨2⋅21+3,2221+3⟩=⟨8,1⟩

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares ⟨8,1⟩, matching option b. This agrees with f_x(2,1)=2·2·√4=8 and f_y(2,1)=4/(2√4)=1.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),\,{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\sqrt{y+3},\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}⟩ \\ ∇f(2,1) & =⟨2\cdot 2\sqrt{1+3},\,\frac{{2}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1+3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Given f(x,y)=sin⁡(xy)+x2ln⁡y, find ∇f(x,y).

a
(ysin⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(xsin⁡(xy)+x2y) j
b
ycos⁡(xy) i+x2y j
c
(ycos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(xcos⁡(xy)+x2y) j
d
(xcos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(ycos⁡(xy)+x2y) j
e
(xsin⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(ysin⁡(xy)+x2y) j
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiating with respect to x gives f_x=y cos(xy)+2x ln(y). Differentiating with respect to y gives f_y=x cos(xy)+x²/y. Thus ∇f=f_x i+f_y j, matching option c.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y})\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given f(x,y)=sin⁡(xy)+x2ln⁡y, find ∇f(x,y).

a
(ysin⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(xsin⁡(xy)+x2y) j
b
ycos⁡(xy) i+x2y j
c
(ycos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(xcos⁡(xy)+x2y) j
d
(xcos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(ycos⁡(xy)+x2y) j
e
(xsin⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(ysin⁡(xy)+x2y) j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂x(sin⁡(xy)+x2ln⁡y)=ycos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡yfy(x,y)=∂∂y(sin⁡(xy)+x2ln⁡y)=xcos⁡(xy)+x2⋅1y=xcos⁡(xy)+x2y

Hence, the gradient is:

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y) i+fy(x,y) j=(ycos⁡(xy)+2xln⁡y) i+(xcos⁡(xy)+x2y) j

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y})\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∇h(x,y,z) at the point (12,1,π) if h(x,y,z)=exycos⁡(yz).

a
e(−i+πj−k)
b
−e(i+12j)
c
e(i−12j+k)
d
−e(i+πj−k)
e

decision.explanation: h_x=ye^{xy}cos(yz), h_y=e^{xy}(x cos(yz)-z sin(yz)), and h_z=-ye^{xy}sin(yz). At (1/2,1,π), cos(π)=-1 and sin(π)=0, giving ∇h=-√e i-(√e/2)j, which matches option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)+{e}^{xy}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))(z) \\  & ={e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,j+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+{e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k \\  & ={e}^{xy}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k) \\ ∇h(\frac{1}{2},1,\pi ) & ={e}^{(1/2)(1)}(1\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )\,i+(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi ))\,j-1\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi )\,k) \\  & =\sqrt{e}(-i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-0\,k) \\  & =-\sqrt{e}(i+\frac{1}{2}\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Evaluate ∇h(x,y,z) at the point (12,1,π) if h(x,y,z)=exycos⁡(yz).

a
e(−i+πj−k)
b
−e(i+12j)
c
e(i−12j+k)
d
−e(i+πj−k)
e
e(i−12j)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: hx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(exycos⁡(yz))=yexycos⁡(yz)hy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(exycos⁡(yz))=xexycos⁡(yz)+exy(−sin⁡(yz))(z)=exy(xcos⁡(yz)−zsin⁡(yz))hz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(exycos⁡(yz))=−yexysin⁡(yz)

Therefore, the gradient is ∇h(x,y,z)=hx(x,y,z)i+hx(x,y,z)j+hx(x,y,z)k=yexycos⁡(yz)i+exy(xcos⁡(yz)−zsin⁡(yz))j−yexysin⁡(yz)k=exy(ycos⁡(yz)i+(xcos⁡(yz)−zsin⁡(yz))j−ysin⁡(yz)k)∇h(12,1,π)=e(1/2)(1)(1cos⁡(1π)i+(12cos⁡(1π)−πsin⁡(1π))j−1sin⁡(1π)k)=e(−i−12j−0k)=−e(i+12j).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)+{e}^{xy}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))(z) \\  & ={e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,j+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+{e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k \\  & ={e}^{xy}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k) \\ ∇h(\frac{1}{2},1,\pi ) & ={e}^{(1/2)(1)}(1\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )\,i+(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi ))\,j-1\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi )\,k) \\  & =\sqrt{e}(-i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-0\,k) \\  & =-\sqrt{e}(i+\frac{1}{2}\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

If f(x,y,z)=xy+yz, find ∇f(x,y,z).

a
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+zyz−1k
b
 yxy−1i+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)j+yzln⁡yk
c
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+yzln⁡yk
d
xyln⁡yi+xyln⁡xj+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)k
e
(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)i+xyln⁡yj+yzln⁡zk
Submit

decision.explanation: The partial derivatives are f_x=yx^{y-1}, f_y=x^y ln(x)+zy^{z-1}, and f_z=y^z ln(y). Their vector matches option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+({x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1})j+{y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

If f(x,y,z)=xy+yz, find ∇f(x,y,z).

a
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+zyz−1k
b
 yxy−1i+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)j+yzln⁡yk
c
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+yzln⁡yk
d
xyln⁡yi+xyln⁡xj+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)k
e
(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)i+xyln⁡yj+yzln⁡zk
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(xy+yz)=yxy−1fy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(xy+yz)=xyln⁡x+zyz−1fz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(xy+yz)=yzln⁡y

Hence, the gradient is ∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=yxy−1i+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)j+yzln⁡yk.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares option b, agreeing with the partial derivatives f_x=yx^{y-1}, f_y=x^y ln(x)+zy^{z-1}, and f_z=y^z ln(y).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+({x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1})j+{y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given h(x,y,z)=xyzln⁡(xyz), find ∇h(x,y,z).

a
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)( i+ j+ k)
b
ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)
c
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)(x i+y j+z k)
d
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)(yz i+xz j+xy k)
e
yz i+xz j+xy k
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=xyz. Since d(u ln(u))/du=ln(u)+1 and ∇u=yz i+xz j+xy k, the chain rule gives ∇h=(ln(xyz)+1)(yz i+xz j+xy k), matching option d.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{yz}{xyz} \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xz}{xyz} \\  & =xz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xy}{xyz} \\  & =xy(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{h}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }i+xz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }j+xy(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given h(x,y,z)=xyzln⁡(xyz), find ∇h(x,y,z).

a
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)( i+ j+ k)
b
ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)
c
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)(x i+y j+z k)
d
(ln⁡(xyz)+1)(yz i+xz j+xy k)
e
yz i+xz j+xy k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: hx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(xyzln⁡(xyz))=yzln⁡(xyz)+xyzyzxyz=yz(ln⁡(xyz)+1)hy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(xyzln⁡(xyz))=xzln⁡(xyz)+xyzxzxyz=xz(ln⁡(xyz)+1)hz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(xyzln⁡(xyz))=xyln⁡(xyz)+xyzxyxyz=xy(ln⁡(xyz)+1) Hence, the gradient is: ∇h(x,y,z)=hx(x,y,z) i+hy(x,y,z) j+hz(x,y,z) k=yz(ln⁡(xyz)+1) i+xz(ln⁡(xyz)+1) j+xy(ln⁡(xyz)+1) k=(ln⁡(xyz)+1)(yz i+xz j+xy k).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{yz}{xyz} \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xz}{xyz} \\  & =xz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xy}{xyz} \\  & =xy(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{h}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }i+xz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }j+xy(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9

Evaluate ∇h(x,y,z) at the point (1,−1,π) if h(x,y,z)=sin⁡(xyz).

a
π i+π j+ k
b
π i+π j+π k
c
−π i+π j+ k
d
π i−π j+ k
e
 i−π j+ k
Submit

decision.explanation: ∇h=cos(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k). At (1,-1,π), cos(-π)=-1 and (yz,xz,xy)=(-π,π,-1), so ∇h=π i-π j+k, matching option d.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

 
Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }k \\ ∇h(1,-1,\pi ) & =(-1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }i+(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }j+(1)(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }k \\  & =(-\pi )(-1)\text{ }i+\pi (-1)\text{ }j-(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =\pi \text{ }i-\pi \text{ }j+\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:

before.html:
Question 10
?

Given g(x,y,z)=e2xzsin⁡(y2−1), find ∇g(x,y,z).

a
 2e2xzsin⁡(y2−1) (zi+y j+x k)
b
 2e2xz (zi+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+x k)
c
 zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k
d
 2e2xz (zi+y j+x k)
e
 2e2xz (zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k)
Submit

decision.explanation: The partial derivatives are g_x=2ze^{2xz}sin(y²−1), g_y=2ye^{2xz}cos(y²−1), and g_z=2xe^{2xz}sin(y²−1). Factoring out 2e^{2xz} gives option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }i+2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2xz}\text{ }(z\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)i+y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+x\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Given g(x,y,z)=e2xzsin⁡(y2−1), find ∇g(x,y,z).

a
 2e2xzsin⁡(y2−1) (zi+y j+x k)
b
 2e2xz (zi+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+x k)
c
 zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k
d
 2e2xz (zi+y j+x k)
e
 2e2xz (zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

gx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2ze2xzsin⁡(y2−1)gy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2ye2xzcos⁡(y2−1)gz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2xe2xzsin⁡(y2−1).

Hence, the gradient is: ∇g(x,y,z)=gx(x,y,z) i+gy(x,y,z) j+gz(x,y,z) k=2ze2xzsin⁡(y2−1) i+2ye2xzcos⁡(y2−1) j+2xe2xzsin⁡(y2−1) k=2e2xz (zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k)

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }i+2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2xz}\text{ }(z\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)i+y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+x\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2y-x=0 \\ 2x+y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,0).$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
content.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2y-x=0 \\ 2x+y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,0).$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+2(y-3)^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+2(y-3)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+0 \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2(y-3)^{2}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 2(y-3) \\  & =4(y-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,i+4(y-3)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,i+4(y-3)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}=0 \\ 4(y-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ and from the second equation, we obtain $y=3.$ 

Therefore, $∇f(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,3).$

Hence, ∇f(x,y)=2xx2+1i+4(y−3)j.

Now, we solve ∇f(x,y)=0:

2xx2+1i+4(y−3)j=0 i+0 j

So, by equating the coefficients of i and j, we obtain:

{2xx2+1=04(y−3)=0

From the first equation, we get x=0 and from the second equation, we obtain y=3.

Therefore, ∇f(x,y)=0 at the point (0,3).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
content.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+2(y-3)^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+2(y-3)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+0 \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2(y-3)^{2}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 2(y-3) \\  & =4(y-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,i+4(y-3)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,i+4(y-3)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}=0 \\ 4(y-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ and from the second equation, we obtain $y=3.$ 

Therefore, $∇f(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,3).$

decision.explanation: Setting f_x=2x−2cos(y)=0 and f_y=2x sin(y)=0 gives x=cos(y) and either x=0 or sin(y)=0. For 0≤y<π, these yield (0,π/2) and (1,0), respectively.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

2(x−cos⁡y)i+2xsin⁡yj=0 i+0 j

So, by equating the coefficients of i and j, we obtain:

{2(x−cos⁡y)=02xsin⁡y=0

Therefore, ∇h(x,y)=0, for 0≤y<π, at two points: (1,0) and (0,π2).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
content.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Given h(x,y,z)=xy+xy2+z3. Find the points (x,y,z) where ∇h(x,y,z)=0.

a
(0,0,0) only
b
 (0,−1,0) only
c
 (0,0,0) and (−1,−1,−1)
d
(0,0,0) and (0,−1,0)
e
 (1,−1,1) only
Submit

decision.explanation: ∇h=⟨y(y+1),x(1+2y),3z²⟩. Setting these components to zero gives y=0 or −1, z=0, and x=0 in either case. Thus the points are (0,0,0) and (0,−1,0).

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =y+{y}^{2}+0 \\  & =y+{y}^{2} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =x+2xy+0 \\  & =x+2xy \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =0+0+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=(y+{y}^{2})\,i+(x+2xy)\,j+3{z}^{2}\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+{y}^{2})\,i+(x+2xy)\,j+3{z}^{2}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y+{y}^{2}=0 \\ x+2xy=0 \\ 3{z}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The first equation can be written as $y(1+y)=0$, which gives $y=0$ or $y=-1.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2x(0) & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

or,

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2x(-1) & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the third equation, we get $z=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,-1,0).$

{y+y2=0x+2xy=03z2=0

Finally, from the third equation, we get z=0.

Therefore, ∇h(x,y,z)=0 at two points: (0,0,0) and (0,−1,0).

Given that g(x,y,z)=xln⁡x+yln⁡y+zln⁡z−x−y−z, find the points (x,y,z) where ∇g(x,y,z)=0.

a
(e,e,e)
b
(0,0,0)
c
(1e,1e,1e)
d
(1,1,1)
e
(−1,−1,−1)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since d(t ln(t)−t)/dt=ln(t), ∇g=⟨ln(x),ln(y),ln(z)⟩. All three components vanish exactly when x=y=z=1, matching option d.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇g(x,y,z)=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
content.problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇g(x,y,z)=0.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j \\  & =[y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+y\text{ }i]+[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+x\text{ }j] \\  & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }i+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
content.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j \\  & =[y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+y\text{ }i]+[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+x\text{ }j] \\  & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }i+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j \\  & =[y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+y\text{ }i]+[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+x\text{ }j] \\  & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }i+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and g(x,y) is given by:

∇[fg]=g∇f+f∇g

So, using this product rule we obtain:

Question 17
?

Find the gradient of the product g(x,y)h(x,y), given that g(x,y)=exy,∇g(x,y)=yexy i+xexy j,h(x,y)=x2+y2,∇h(x,y)=2x i+2y j.

a
(x2y+y3)exy i+(x3+xy2)exy j
b
(x2y+y3+2x)exy i+(x3+xy2+2y)exy j
c
(x2y+y3+2x) i+(x3+xy2+2y) j
d
(x2+y2+2x)exy i+(x2+y2+2y)exy j
e
2xexy i+2yexy j
Submit

decision.explanation: Using ∇(gh)=h∇g+g∇h, the i component is e^{xy}[y(x²+y²)+2x], and the j component is e^{xy}[x(x²+y²)+2y]. Expanding gives option b.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[gh]=h\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j)+{e}^{xy}(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j) \\  & =(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j)+(2x{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{xy}\text{ }j) \\  & =({x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}+2x){e}^{xy}\text{ }i+({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 17

Find the gradient of the product g(x,y)h(x,y), given that g(x,y)=exy,∇g(x,y)=yexy i+xexy j,h(x,y)=x2+y2,∇h(x,y)=2x i+2y j.

a
(x2y+y3)exy i+(x3+xy2)exy j
b
(x2y+y3+2x)exy i+(x3+xy2+2y)exy j
c
(x2y+y3+2x) i+(x3+xy2+2y) j
d
(x2+y2+2x)exy i+(x2+y2+2y)exy j
e
2xexy i+2yexy j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions g(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by:

∇[gh]=h∇g+g∇h

Using the product rule, we obtain:

∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)]=h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y)=(x2+y2)(yexy i+xexy j)+exy(2x i+2y j)=((x2+y2)yexy i+(x2+y2)xexy j)+(2xexy i+2yexy j)=(x2y+y3+2x)exy i+(x3+xy2+2y)exy j

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares option b. The product rule ∇(gh)=h∇g+g∇h gives e^{xy}[y(x²+y²)+2x]i+e^{xy}[x(x²+y²)+2y]j, confirming its stated result.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
content.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[gh]=h\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j)+{e}^{xy}(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j) \\  & =(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})y{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})x{e}^{xy}\text{ }j)+(2x{e}^{xy}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{xy}\text{ }j) \\  & =({x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}+2x){e}^{xy}\text{ }i+({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find the gradient of the product g(x,y)h(x,y), given that g(x,y)=ex−y,∇g(x,y)=ex−yi−ex−yj,h(x,y)=x2−3xy,∇h(x,y)=(2x−3y)i−3xj.

a
 ex−y((x2−3xy)i−3xj)
b
 ex−y((x2−3xy+2x−3y)i−(x2−3xy+3x)j)
c
 ex−y((2x−3y)i−3xj)
d
 ex−y((x2−3xy−2x−3y)i+(x2+3xy+3x)j)
e
 ex−y((x2−3xy−y)i+(x2+3xy+3x)j)
Submit

decision.explanation: The product rule gives ∇(gh)=h∇g+g∇h=e^{x−y}[(x²−3xy+2x−3y)i−(x²−3xy+3x)j], matching option b.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{x-y},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-3xy,\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=(2x-3y)\,i-3x\,j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[gh]=h∇g+g∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}-3xy)({e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j)+{e}^{x-y}((2x-3y)\,i-3x\,j) \\  & =(({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\,i-({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\,j)+((2x-3y){e}^{x-y}\,i-3x{e}^{x-y}\,j) \\  & ={e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\,i-{e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}(({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\,i-({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find the gradient of the product g(x,y)h(x,y), given that g(x,y)=ex−y,∇g(x,y)=ex−yi−ex−yj,h(x,y)=x2−3xy,∇h(x,y)=(2x−3y)i−3xj.

a
 ex−y((x2−3xy)i−3xj)
b
 ex−y((x2−3xy+2x−3y)i−(x2−3xy+3x)j)
c
 ex−y((2x−3y)i−3xj)
d
 ex−y((x2−3xy−2x−3y)i+(x2+3xy+3x)j)
e
 ex−y((x2−3xy−y)i+(x2+3xy+3x)j)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions g(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[gh]=h∇g+g∇h.

Using the product rule, we obtain ∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)]=h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y)=(x2−3xy)(ex−yi−ex−yj)+ex−y((2x−3y)i−3xj)=((x2−3xy)ex−yi−(x2−3xy)ex−yj)+((2x−3y)ex−yi−3xex−yj)=ex−y(x2−3xy+2x−3y)i−ex−y(x2−3xy+3x)j=ex−y((x2−3xy+2x−3y)i−(x2−3xy+3x)j).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
content.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{x-y},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-3xy,\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=(2x-3y)\,i-3x\,j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[gh]=h∇g+g∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}-3xy)({e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j)+{e}^{x-y}((2x-3y)\,i-3x\,j) \\  & =(({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\,i-({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\,j)+((2x-3y){e}^{x-y}\,i-3x{e}^{x-y}\,j) \\  & ={e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\,i-{e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}(({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\,i-({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z), given that f(x,y,z)=xy2z3,∇f(x,y,z)=y2z3i+2xyz3j+3xy2z2k,h(x,y,z)=1xyz,∇h(x,y,z)=−1x2yzi−1xy2zj−1xyz2 k.

a
xi−2xzk
b
z2j+2yzk
c
3xi+y2j−2xyk
d
y2i+3xyk
e
xi−z2j−2yzk

decision.explanation: On the domain xyz≠0, the product simplifies to fh=yz². Therefore ∇(fh)=0i+z²j+2yzk, matching option b.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\, &  & ∇f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k, &  &  \\ h(x,y,z) & =\frac{1}{xyz},\, &  & ∇h(x,y,z)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\text{ }k. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{1}{xyz}({y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k)+x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,i+\frac{2xy{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,j+\frac{3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{xyz}\,k-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k \\  & =\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i+2{z}^{2}\,j+3yz\,k-\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i-{z}^{2}\,j-yz\,k \\  & ={z}^{2}\,j+2yz\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.

Using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)]=h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)=1xyz(y2z3i+2xyz3j+3xy2z2k)+xy2z3(−1x2yzi−1xy2zj−1xyz2k)=y2z3xyzi+2xyz3xyzj+3xy2z2xyzk−xy2z3x2yzi−xy2z3xy2zj−xy2z3xyz2k=yz2xi+2z2j+3yzk−yz2xi−z2j−yzk=z2j+2yzk.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
content.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\, &  & ∇f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k, &  &  \\ h(x,y,z) & =\frac{1}{xyz},\, &  & ∇h(x,y,z)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\text{ }k. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{1}{xyz}({y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k)+x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,i+\frac{2xy{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,j+\frac{3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{xyz}\,k-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k \\  & =\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i+2{z}^{2}\,j+3yz\,k-\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i-{z}^{2}\,j-yz\,k \\  & ={z}^{2}\,j+2yz\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }i+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }i+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }j \\  & =\text{ }i+\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

a
y i+x j

x i+y j

Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by:

∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h

Using the product rule, we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)]=h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y)=1xy((2xy+y2) i+(x2+2xy) j)+(x2y+xy2)(−1x2y i−1xy2 j)=(2xy+y2xy i+x2+2xyxy j)+(−x2y+xy2x2y i−x2y+xy2xy2 j)=(2x+yx i+x+2yy j)+(−x+yx i−x+yy j)=(−x+yx+2x+yx) i+(−x+yy+x+2yy) j= i+ j

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
content.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }i+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }i+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }j \\  & =\text{ }i+\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$
